analysis.one_liner: Requires public disclosure of fracking chemicals and ends oil and gas exemptions from key environmental laws.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2018, the bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require oil and gas companies to disclose, on a public website, the chemicals they use in hydraulic fracturing before and after drilling, and to test nearby water before drilling on federal lands. It would also strip away special exemptions that let oil and gas operations bypass parts of the Safe Drinking Water Act, the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act, and the hazardous-waste law. The measure died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink the water or breathe the air around drilling sites: they would learn which chemicals are being pumped underground, and the operations would have to meet the same drinking-water, air, and hazardous-waste rules that apply to other industries. Communities on or near federal lands would get baseline water testing before drilling begins.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracking sites and federal-land communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires companies to publicly disclose the chemicals used in each fracking operation before drilling starts and within 30 days after it ends, including chemical identities, safety data sheets, and volumes, posted on a public website [S3].
It requires baseline water testing before fracking begins under federal oil and gas leases, and reinstates the 2015 federal fracking rule on those lands until new regulations are issued [S3].

It removes the exemption that currently keeps fracking out of the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground injection program, subjecting it to the same permitting regime as other underground injection [S3].

It removes exemptions from Clean Water Act stormwater permits, Clean Air Act rules for aggregated oil and gas emissions (and adds hydrogen sulfide as a hazardous air pollutant), and requires the EPA to evaluate whether drilling fluids and produced waters should be regulated as hazardous waste with groundwater monitoring and financial assurance at disposal sites [S3].
In a medical emergency, treating physicians and nurses can obtain the identity of trade-secret fracking chemicals without a confidentiality agreement in place first [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers bear the direct cost: permitting under the Safe Drinking Water Act, public chemical disclosure, water testing before drilling on federal lands, air permits, and stricter waste handling. Some costs would likely be passed to consumers through higher energy prices, and some marginal drilling on federal lands might become uneconomical.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers, and some energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The disclosure requirements still allow companies to shield proprietary chemical formulas from public release; the public would get chemical identities in many cases, but a trade-secret carve-out remains, with full formula disclosure only when a doctor declares a medical emergency [S3].

The compliance costs fall on a domestic industry that supplies heating fuel, electricity generation, and industrial feedstocks, and companies would likely pass some portion of those costs to households through energy prices.

The bill does not fund the added water testing, permitting, or monitoring work at the EPA, the Department of the Interior, or the states, leaving agencies to absorb the workload within existing budgets [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is information and protection: people near drilling would finally know what chemicals are being injected under them, and the largest industrial exemptions from water, air, and waste law would close. The costs are real but ordinary for environmental regulation, borne mainly by producers and only partly passed to consumers. The main design weakness is the trade-secret carve-out, which keeps full chemical formulas out of public view except in emergencies.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, and then to a subcommittee, and stayed there until the session ended — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Darren Soto introduced the bill on September 10, 2018, with seven original cosponsors, all Democrats [S5].
It was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Natural Resources Committees [S5].

On September 19, 2018, it was referred to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and no further action of any kind followed for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019 [S5].

The bill's substantive provisions would have required chemical disclosure, federal-land fracking rules, and repeal of oil and gas exemptions under the Safe Drinking Water Act, Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, and Solid Waste Disposal Act [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, which avoided federal chemical disclosure, drinking-water permitting, air permits, and stricter waste rules. Nothing in the record shows the industry acted on this bill; it simply never moved in a Republican-controlled House.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers, by avoiding new regulation

industries.note: The bill closes exemptions that currently let fracking bypass the Safe Drinking Water Act, Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, and hazardous-waste law, and forces public chemical disclosure and pre-drilling water testing. Those compliance costs come directly out of operating margins, so the industry's financial interest runs against the community right-to-know and water protections the bill provides.

industries.industry: Waste disposal facilities handling drilling fluids and produced water
industries.note: The bill directs the EPA to decide whether oil and gas wastes are hazardous and to set groundwater monitoring, siting, and financial-assurance criteria for facilities receiving them. It would raise disposal costs but also bring drilling-waste disposal under enforceable federal standards.
